newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore curbs Queens Counsels in criminal cases.
newsitem.headline: Singapore curbs Queens Counsels in criminal cases.

text.p: Singapore on Thursday took a further step towards barring Queens Counsels (QCs) in criminal cases by requiring an applicant to give a special reason to justify their admission.

It would be up to the courts to determine what the "special reason" was before admitting QCs, according to an amended bill passed by parliament. QCs are senior lawyers from Britain and certain other Commonwealth countries.

"Eventually, we should do away with representation by QCs in criminal cases," Law Minister S. Jayakumar said. "This should be looked at again when we have an adequate number of Senior Counsel practising at the Criminal Bar."
He said the Senate of Singapore's Academy of Law was about to appoint its equivalent of QCs, namely Senior Counsels.

Jayakumar said that except for basic principles, Singapore's criminal process and criminal law were different from the English system. Singapore's penal code was based on Indian law and not the English model, he added.
"QCs in general are not familiar with our criminal justice system," he said. "As a result, we have experienced some cases of our criminal justice system being distorted in the foreign media."
He said since 1991 Singapore has admitted only 10 QCs in criminal cases and in the nine cases they dealt with, only two were successful.
A curb on QCs was first made in 1991, when the condition was imposed that the court must be satisfied that the case was of "sufficient difficulty and complexity" to admit a QC.
The policy then was that QCs should only be admitted for complex and difficult cases where the necessary knowledge or experience was not available from local lawyers, Jayakumar said.
The intention was to favour the admission of QCs in banking and commercial cases. The latest amendment does not affect admission of QCs in civil cases.
Jayakumar said there should be less need now for QCs in criminal cases with improvements in advocacy skills and experience among local lawyers in the past five years.
There are currently 89 local criminal lawyers designated as senior lawyers and 125 as junior lawyers.
